title: Ordinary and completed tensor with an integral coefficient line
statement:
Let $\ell$ be prime, $E/\mathbf Q_\ell$ a finite extension with valuation ring $\mathcal O_E$ and uniformizer $\varpi$, and $X$ a scheme on which $\ell$ is invertible. On its small pro-etale site put $R=\widehat{\mathcal O}_{E,X}=\varprojlim_n(\mathcal O_E/\varpi^n)_X$ [def-weil-completed-integral-coefficients]. Let $C\in D(R)$ be derived complete [def-weil-derived-complete], and let $T$ be an $R$-module sheaf locally isomorphic to $R$ and placed in degree zero. Use the ordinary derived tensor $\otimes_R^L$ in $D(R)$, the total tensor complex [def-pc-tensor-complex-sheaves] over $R$ after K-flat replacement of the first factor [def-pc-kflat-complex], and the completed tensor $\widehat\otimes^L$ defined by the functorial reduction-tower cone construction of [def-pur-integral-derived-operations]. Write $C_n=C\otimes_R^L(R/\varpi^n)$, $T_n=T\otimes_R(R/\varpi^n)$, and regard each finite reduction as an $R$-complex by restriction of scalars. The natural reduction maps induce an isomorphism
$$
C\otimes_R^L T\xrightarrow{\sim}R\varprojlim_n(C_n\otimes_{R/\varpi^n}^L T_n)=C\widehat\otimes^L T.
$$
Here the comparison is obtained on a K-flat representative $P\to C$ by the canonical map from $P\otimes_R T$ to the shifted cone of $1-s$ on the products of its reductions. It is natural in $C$ and in isomorphisms of such $T$, and its reduction at every $n$ is the ordinary tensor/reduction identification.

source.place: Definition 3.4.10, Lemma 3.4.12(4), Proposition 3.5.1 and Definition 3.5.2; specialization to a locally free rank-one completed coefficient sheaf, as required by thm-sf-dual-perfect.proof.md Step 4

proof.text: First identify the finite coefficient sheaves used by the two constructions. By [lem-weil-l-adic-extension-integers-dvr], $\mathcal O_E$ is a principal ideal domain, hence Noetherian since every ideal has one generator. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-completed-constant-sheaf-reduction] with $A=\mathcal O_E$, $I=(\varpi)$ and $T=X$. It gives the canonical isomorphism $R\otimes^L_{(\mathcal O_E)_X}(\mathcal O_E/\varpi^n)_X\cong(\mathcal O_E/\varpi^n)_X$. Taking degree-zero cohomology identifies the ordinary tensor, which is the cokernel of multiplication by $\varpi^n$ on $R$, with $(\mathcal O_E/\varpi^n)_X$. Thus $R_n:=R/\varpi^nR=(\mathcal O_E/\varpi^n)_X$, with the actual quotient maps and their transitions. All subsequent tensors of sheaves are over $R$ or $R_n$, not over the discrete constant integral sheaf.

source.place: Tag 093M, lemma-completion-flat, applied to powers of the uniformizer

proof.text: The functor $F_T:M\mapsto M\otimes_R T$ on module sheaves is exact: on a cover trivializing $T$ it is identified with the identity, so the kernels and images of the tensored sequence agree locally. Restriction to a slice is exact by [lem-pur-site-restriction-module-adjunction-exact], and a sheaf vanishing on a covering family vanishes. For any countable family $(M_i)$, let $b:(\prod_iM_i)\otimes_R T\to\prod_i(M_i\otimes_R T)$ have components $\mathrm{pr}_i\otimes1$. Products are sectionwise by [lem-weil-proetale-countable-products-exact], so restricting a product to each trivializing slice gives the product of the restrictions. On that slice, if $e$ generates $T$, the map sends $(m_i)_i\otimes ae$ to $(am_i\otimes e)_i$; its inverse sends $(m_i\otimes e)_i$ to $(m_i)_i\otimes e$. Thus $b$ is an isomorphism. These are statements about the displayed canonical map, so they do not depend on a generator. The same arguments apply to $T_n$ over $R_n$. In particular $T[0]$ and $T_n[0]$ are K-flat: tensoring any acyclic complex by either sheaf preserves its zero cohomology.

source.place: Definition 3.4.10; elementary local rank-one tensor calculation, using sectionwise products

proof.text:
Choose $P\to C$ K-flat with flat terms by [lem-pc-kflat-resolution]. Put $P_n=P\otimes_RR_n$. By [lem-pur-kflat-change-of-rings], $P_n$ is K-flat with flat terms over $R_n$; it represents $C_n$ by [lem-pur-derived-change-of-rings]. Step 2 shows that $T$ and $T_n$ themselves can be used as their K-flat resolutions in [def-pur-integral-derived-operations]. Hence the ordinary tensor is represented by $P\otimes_RT$, and the completed tensor is represented by $\operatorname{Cone}(1-s:\prod_n(P_n\otimes_{R_n}T_n)\to\prod_n(P_n\otimes_{R_n}T_n))[-1]$. The termwise isomorphism
$$(P\otimes_RT)\otimes_RR_n\longrightarrow P_n\otimes_{R_n}T_n,\qquad (p\otimes t)\otimes a\longmapsto(p\otimes a)\otimes(t\otimes1)$$
has inverse $(p\otimes a)\otimes(t\otimes b)\mapsto(p\otimes t)\otimes ab$. Balancing proves that these are inverse, and both commute with differentials and quotient transitions. The same formulas identify the augmentation from $P\otimes T$ with reduction in each level.

source.place: Tags 06YS, 0G7E and 06YY; tensor-balancing formulas for the quotient maps

proof.text:
Apply [lem-weil-finite-free-completed-scalar-comparison] to the identity extension $E\subset E$ on $X$ and the given derived-complete $C$. Its last sentence gives that the specific augmentation
$$\alpha_P:P\longrightarrow\operatorname{Cone}(1-s:\prod_nP_n\to\prod_nP_n)[-1]$$
with product component $(P\to P_n)_n$ and zero shifted-product component is an isomorphism in $D(R)$. The coefficient identification in step 1 identifies its tower with this one. This application uses neither boundedness nor constructibility nor quasi-compactness of $X$. In particular it uses the statement about the canonical map in that cited node, rather than choosing an unspecified lift into a triangulated derived limit.

source.place: Lemma 3.4.12(4), Proposition 3.5.1 and Definition 3.5.2; canonical completion comparison, identity-extension specialization

proof.text: Apply the exact functor $F_T$ of step 2 termwise to $\alpha_P$. It preserves quasi-isomorphisms because it preserves the kernels and images computing cohomology; thus $F_T(\alpha_P)$ is an isomorphism in $D(R)$. The isomorphism $b$ of step 2 in every cochain degree commutes with $1-s$: its $n$th component is projection followed by tensoring the transition with $1_T$ on either side. Tensoring with $T[0]$ also commutes with the shifted cone, directly from its finite direct sums and the same signed differential. Consequently $F_T$ identifies the target of $F_T(\alpha_P)$ with $\operatorname{Cone}(1-s:\prod_n(P_n\otimes_RT)\to\prod_n(P_n\otimes_RT))[-1]$. Balancing identifies $P_n\otimes_RT$ with $P_n\otimes_{R_n}T_n$ as in step 3. Under this composite, the product component of $F_T(\alpha_P)$ is precisely the tensor/reduction augmentation and its shifted-product component remains zero. This is exactly the comparison specified in the item, and proves it is an isomorphism. The well-definedness assertion of [lem-pur-integral-operations-well-defined] identifies this cone with the specified completed tensor, independently of resolutions.

source.place: Definition 3.4.10 and Lemma 3.4.12(4); explicit tensor of the functorial reduction-tower cone

proof.text: All displayed formulas commute with chain maps of $P$ and with sheaf isomorphisms $T\to T'$, and the product and cone constructions are functorial in these strictly commuting maps. For a quasi-isomorphism between K-flat resolutions, its cone is acyclic and K-flat; [lem-pur-acyclic-kflat-tensor-arbitrary] shows that ordinary tensor carries it to a quasi-isomorphism. The completed side and its comparison on resolutions descend by [lem-pur-integral-operations-well-defined]. This proves the claimed naturality in $D(R)$. Finally, projecting the cone comparison to level $n$ after the comparison gives exactly $P\otimes_RT\to P_n\otimes_{R_n}T_n$, by its product component. By [lem-pur-sheaf-ring-derived-coefficient-adjunction], its adjoint after derived scalar extension to $R_n$ is represented by $x\otimes a\mapsto a\,\overline{x}$; this is the isomorphism of step 3. Since the comparison itself is an isomorphism, the adjoint of the tower projection from its target is also an isomorphism, and reducing the comparison gives precisely the ordinary tensor/reduction identification. This verifies the finite-reduction clause with the actual projection maps.
